Mathematics at Home and School:
🏠 Mathematics at Home & School 🏫

Math isn't just for tests! It is hidden everywhere in your daily life.

1. Learning Objectives

  • Identify how mathematics is used at home and at school.
  • Count objects and compare quantities.
  • Use addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division in everyday situations.

2. Everyday Mathematics

Mathematics is not only something we learn in a classroom. You are doing math without even realizing it!

  • At home: Counting toys, sharing slices of pizza equally with your siblings, setting the microwave timer, or measuring flour for a cake.
  • At school: Counting the number of students on the bus, arranging desks in neat rows, or reading the daily timetable to see when recess starts!

3. Sharing Equally (Division!)

A teacher has 12 crayons and wants to share them equally among 4 children. How many does each get?

You use Division!
12 ÷ 4 = 3 crayons per child.

⭐ Secret check: You can always check a division problem by using multiplication! 4 children × 3 crayons = 12 crayons total!
Shopping and Comparing Prices:
🛒 Shopping & Comparing Prices 🛒

Become a smart shopper and learn how to stretch your coins!

1. Learning Objectives

  • Read and understand price labels.
  • Compare prices to find the cheaper item.
  • Calculate the total cost of several items and the change received.
  • Compare pack sizes to find the best value.

2. Finding the Total Cost

When buying several items, you add their prices together.
If an apple costs 5 coins and a notebook costs 12 coins, the total is:
12 + 5 = 17 coins.

3. Calculating Change

Change is the money the cashier returns to you when you hand them more money than the item actually costs!

If your total is 17 coins, and you hand the cashier a 20-coin note, how much change do you get?
20 − 17 = 3 coins in change!

4. Value for Money

The pack with the cheapest sticker isn't always the best deal! You have to compare the "cost per item".

  • Pack A: 4 pencils for 8 coins. (8 ÷ 4 = 2 coins per pencil).
  • Pack B: 3 pencils for 6 coins. (6 ÷ 3 = 2 coins per pencil).

They actually offer the exact same value! Pack A costs more in total, but only because it has an extra pencil in it.
Planning a Simple Budget:
🐷 Planning a Simple Budget 🐷

Make a master plan for your money before it disappears!

My Field Trip Budget
Total Money:30 Coins
Lunch Expense:− 12 Coins
Drink Expense:− 4 Coins
Money Remaining:14 Coins

1. Learning Objectives

  • Explain what a budget is and why it is useful.
  • List planned expenses and calculate their total.
  • Work out how much money remains.

2. What is a Budget?

A budget is a strict plan for how to use your money. It helps you figure out exactly what you can afford and stops you from accidentally spending too much!

A simple budget has three main parts:

  1. Money Available: The total amount of coins in your pocket.
  2. Expenses: The money you plan to spend.
  3. Remaining Balance: The money left over (which you can save for later!).

3. Needs vs. Wants

When making a budget, it helps to understand the difference between Needs and Wants.

  • Needs are things necessary for survival or for a specific task (like buying lunch on a school trip, or buying a pencil for an exam).
  • Wants are fun things you would enjoy, but don't absolutely need right away (like an extra toy).

⚠️ Over Budget: What happens if you only have 25 coins, but your planned expenses add up to 29? You are 4 coins over budget! You must review your plan and remove a "Want" from your list!
Measuring Objects and Spaces:
📏 Measuring Objects and Spaces 📏

Find out exactly how long, heavy, and full the world is!

1. Learning Objectives

  • Identify suitable units for measuring length, height, and distance.
  • Measure objects correctly using rulers.
  • Calculate the perimeter of simple shapes.

2. Units of Length

We use different units depending on how big the object is!

  • Millimetres (mm) & Centimetres (cm): Used for small things, like the length of a pencil or a bug!
  • Metres (m): Used for larger things, like the height of a door or the length of a swimming pool.
  • Kilometres (km): Used for huge distances, like the road between two cities!

Magic Conversions: 1 metre = 100 centimetres. 1 kilometre = 1000 metres.

3. The Number One Ruler Mistake

When measuring an object with a ruler, you MUST line up the edge of the object with the Zero (0) mark, NOT the edge of the physical ruler! If your ruler is broken and you have to start at the 2cm mark and end at the 8cm mark, you have to subtract to find the real length: 8 − 2 = 6cm.

4. Perimeter (The Outside Edge)

The perimeter is the total distance walking all the way around the outside edge of a flat shape.

If a rectangular garden is 6m long and 3m wide, you have to add up all 4 sides!
6 + 6 + 3 + 3 = 18 metres.
Cooking and Understanding Quantities:
🍳 Cooking and Understanding Quantities 🍳

Math is the secret ingredient in every delicious recipe!

1. Learning Objectives

  • Measure ingredients using common units.
  • Add and subtract ingredient amounts.
  • Double or halve simple recipe quantities.

2. The Kitchen Measurement Units

In the kitchen, we use totally different tools to measure dry food versus wet food!

  • Mass (Weight): We use Grams (g) and Kilograms (kg) to measure dry, solid things like flour, sugar, or rice.
  • Volume (Liquid Capacity): We use Millilitres (mL) and Litres (L) to measure wet things that flow, like milk, water, or oil.

⚠️ Important: You cannot add grams and millilitres together! They measure completely different things.

3. Doubling a Recipe

If you have a recipe that makes food for 2 people, but you want to invite 2 more friends, you need to make twice as much food! To do this, you just multiply every ingredient by 2.

Original RecipeDoubled Recipe (× 2)
2 cups of flour4 cups of flour
1 cup of milk2 cups of milk
3 eggs6 eggs

4. Halving a Recipe

If you only want to make a tiny snack, you can halve the recipe by dividing every ingredient by 2!

If a recipe calls for 400g of sugar, and you halve the recipe:
400 ÷ 2 = 200g of sugar.
Travel Distance and Journey Time:
🚗 Travel Distance and Journey Time 🚗

How far is it, and how long will it take to get there?

1. Learning Objectives

  • Identify units used to measure travel distance and time.
  • Calculate how long a journey takes.
  • Work out arrival times and departure times.

2. Measuring Distance

We use different units depending on how far we have to walk or drive.

  • Metres (m): For short distances, like walking across the playground.
  • Kilometres (km): For huge distances, like driving to a whole new city! (1 km = 1000 metres).

3. Measuring Journey Time

To find out exactly how long you were sitting in the car, you subtract the Departure Time from the Arrival Time.

If the bus leaves at 09:15 and arrives at 10:00, count up the minutes:
From 09:15 to 09:30 is 15 minutes.
From 09:30 to 10:00 is 30 minutes.
Total: 15 + 30 = 45 minutes!

4. Finding the Arrival Time

If you know what time you are leaving, and you know how long the trip takes, you can predict exactly when you will arrive by adding!

A walk starts at 10:20 and takes 35 minutes.
10:20 + 30 minutes = 10:50.
10:50 + 5 more minutes = 10:55!

⚠️ Clock Warning: Remember that time doesn't count up to 100! There are only 60 minutes in an hour. So 10:50 + 20 minutes does NOT equal 10:70. It rolls over to 11:10!
Reading Everyday Tables, Charts and Sign:
📊 Reading Tables, Charts and Signs 📊

Decoding the information hidden on walls and screens all around us!

1. Learning Objectives

  • Understand common signs, symbols, and numerical information.
  • Read information from simple tables.
  • Interpret bar charts and picture graphs.

2. Reading Everyday Signs

Numbers are painted everywhere in the real world! You have to understand the context to know what the number means.

  • Speed Limit Signs: A big red circle with "30" means cars cannot go faster than 30 km/h.
  • Price Labels: A tag on a shelf with "$12.50" tells you exactly how much money you need to hand to the cashier.
  • Elevator Signs: Arrows and digital numbers tell you if the metal box is going Up or Down, and what floor it is currently on!

3. Finding Totals in Tables

Sometimes you need to do a little math to answer a question based on a chart.

A shop sells the following sandwiches in one hour:

  • Cheese: 12
  • Egg: 9
  • Vegetable: 7

Question: How many more cheese sandwiches than vegetable sandwiches were sold?
Math: 12 − 7 = 5.
Answer: 5 more cheese sandwiches were sold!
Estimation in Everyday Situations:
🎯 Estimation in Everyday Situations 🎯

How to make a brilliant, educated guess when you don't have a calculator or ruler!

1. Learning Objectives

  • Explain what estimation means.
  • Round numbers to make calculations incredibly easy.
  • Use estimation to check whether an answer is reasonable.

2. What is Estimation?

Estimation means finding a quick answer that is close to the exact value, without needing to calculate or measure everything perfectly.

We estimate all the time! Like guessing how many people are in a room, or predicting how many minutes it will take to walk to the park.

3. Estimating by Rounding

Rounding replaces an ugly, complicated number with a nearby, friendly number (usually one that ends in zero!).

  • If the end digit is 0, 1, 2, 3, or 4, let it rest! (Round DOWN). Example: 23 becomes 20.
  • If the end digit is 5, 6, 7, 8, or 9, push it up! (Round UP). Example: 78 becomes 80.

4. Catching Huge Mistakes!

Estimation is your best defense against silly calculator mistakes.

Suppose you buy two toys that cost 49 coins and 32 coins. You do the math fast and think the total is 171 coins. Is that right?

Do a quick mental estimate by rounding:
49 is about 50. 32 is about 30.
50 + 30 = 80.

Since 80 is nowhere near 171, you instantly know your first math answer was unreasonable (totally wrong!). The exact total was actually 81. Estimation just saved you from paying way too much!
Solving Real-Life Multi-Step Problems:
🧩 Solving Real-Life Multi-Step Problems 🧩

Break big challenges down into small, conquerable steps!

1. Learning Objectives

  • Identify the information needed to solve a real-life problem.
  • Solve problems that require two or more mathematical steps.
  • Organise calculations in a sensible order.

2. What is a Multi-Step Problem?

A multi-step problem is a math puzzle hiding inside a story! It requires more than one calculation to find the final answer.

3. The 4-Step Strategy

  1. Read & Identify: Find the important numbers. What are they asking you to find out?
  2. Plan: Decide if you need to add, subtract, multiply, or divide. What goes first?
  3. Calculate: Do the math for Step 1. Then use that answer to do the math for Step 2.
  4. Check: Does your final answer make logical sense in the real world?

4. Worked Example: Sharing Objects

The Story: A teacher has 4 boxes containing 6 pencils each. The teacher gives 5 pencils to another class. How many pencils remain?

  • Step 1 (Find the total starting pencils): We have 4 groups of 6.
    4 × 6 = 24 pencils.
  • Step 2 (Subtract the pencils given away): Now take away the 5.
    24 − 5 = 19 pencils.

Answer: 19 pencils remain!

⚠️ Important: The order matters! If you subtracted 5 from 6 first, the whole answer would be a disaster! Always think about the story happening in real-time.
Choosing the Right Mathematical Operatio:
➕ Choosing the Right Operation ➗

Translating English words into Math symbols!

1. Learning Objectives

  • Identify when to use addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division.
  • Recognise common words that act as clues.
  • Translate everyday problems into mathematical calculations.

2. The Four Secret Weapons

Mathematics uses four basic operations to solve almost every problem in the world!

OperationWhat it doesClue Words to look for
Addition (+)Combines amounts to find a total.altogether, total, combined, more added
Subtraction (−)Finds what remains or the difference.left, remaining, difference, how many fewer
Multiplication (×)Finds the total in equal groups.equal groups, each, total of identical items
Division (÷)Shares an amount equally.shared equally, per group, split equally

3. Be Careful with Clues!

Clue words are helpful, but the meaning of the whole story matters more than any single word!

Example 1: A shop has 6 boxes containing 8 cups each. How many cups total?
There are equal groups, so you Multiply! 6 × 8 = 48 cups.

Example 2: A shop places 48 cups equally into 6 boxes. How many in each box?
They are sharing a big total into smaller boxes, so you Divide! 48 ÷ 6 = 8 cups per box.
Applying Mathematics to Everyday Decisio:
⚖️ Mathematics in Everyday Decisions ⚖️

Using math to make the absolute best choice in the real world!

1. Learning Objectives

  • Use mathematics to compare choices.
  • Compare prices, quantities, and time.
  • Use calculations to make informed, smart decisions.

2. Comparing Value

Every day, we make choices. Math helps us compare the options so we don't get ripped off!

Look at the picture above. Shop A sells one notebook for 12 coins. Shop B sells a pack of two notebooks for 20 coins. Which is the better deal?

  • Shop A price per notebook: 12 coins.
  • Shop B price per notebook: 20 ÷ 2 = 10 coins.

Shop B is a much better deal! A lower total price (12 coins vs 20 coins) does not always mean better value. You have to compare the price for the same quantity.

3. The "Best" Choice isn't just Numbers

Math helps reveal the facts, but your brain has to make the final decision based on real-world constraints!

If you only have 15 coins in your pocket, you physically cannot afford Shop B, even though it's a better deal. You will have to buy from Shop A!

Sometimes the quickest route on a map isn't the safest. Sometimes the cheapest water bottle is too small. A good mathematical decision uses accurate math PLUS sensible real-world reasoning!
